text: A SQL Server login is a name. An Oracle user is a name. A MySQL user is a name and a host pattern together, and that pairing is the single most distinctive thing about MySQL's account model.

Every MySQL account is identified by username and host together. These three CREATE USER statements produce three genuinely separate accounts, even though two share the username app_svc — each one authenticates only from the host pattern it was created with.

The host half changes behavior completely: a specific IP range, localhost only through the Unix socket, or the percent wildcard matching any host at all. When a connection arrives, MySQL authenticates against the most specific user-at-host pattern that matches, not just the first one found.

ALTER USER changes a password or locks an account without deleting it — useful for an employee on leave. DROP USER removes one exact user-at-host pair; a same-named account at a different host is untouched. Every statement must address the full pair, not just a bare username.

Getting the host scope wrong is one of the most common MySQL security mistakes a DBA coming from another platform makes. Next up: privileges — GRANT and REVOKE, and MySQL's global, database, table, and column-level scopes.
